newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, EU officials fail to solve Cuba issues.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, EU officials fail to solve Cuba issues.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and top European Union officials met on Monday to discuss a U.S. law punishing some foreign firms for doing business with Cuba but failed to resolve their impasse.

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, the current president of the EU Council of Ministers, and European Commission President Jacques Santer met Clinton at the White House for talks aiming to defuse tensions over the so-called "Helms-Burton" law.

Clinton -- praising the EU for calling for democracy in Cuba, where Fidel Castro leads one of the world's last communist regimes -- said it shows "that we are now working together to promote freedom and democracy in Cuba."
During a joint news conference, Bruton said: "There is ... a difference in method, but there is absolutely no difference in objective within the European Union and the United States on Cuba."

"We have helped clear the air on Cuba," added Santer, but Clinton made clear he has made no decision on whether or not he will continue to delay implementing the provision in the law that has outraged most allies.

In addition to expanding the 34-year-old U.S. embargo on Cuba, the law allows lawsuits to be filed in U.S. courts against foreign firms that own or operate properties seized by Cuba from U.S. citizens who were Cuban nationals before Fidel Castro came to power in 1959.

Saying the EU would continue to press its challenge to the law before the World Trade Organization, Santer noted that "Europe will remain firmly opposed to all extra-territorial legislation, whatever its source."

The European Union has threatened to retailiate against American firms if any of its businesses suffer from the law. It was passed in March shortly after four Cuban-American exiles were killed when Cuban MiGs shot down two small U.S. civilian aircraft they were flying off the coast of Cuba.

In July, Clinton ordered the sanctions to come into force, but delayed implementation for six months to calm angry allies in Europe as well as Canada and Mexico. He must decide by Jan. 16 whether the delay should be extended.

The law also denies U.S. visas to shareholders and officers of foreign firms operating the seized properties in Cuba. The provision already has been used against officers of a Canadian mining company and a Mexican telecommunications firm.

In a communique following an EU summit in Dublin that ended on Saturday, EU leaders scolded Washington, saying it should pursue means against Cuba "other than unilateral action at the expense of closer partners with shared values."

Emphasizing Europe's different approach to Cuba, the European Union said it would consider negotiating a trade accord with Havana, making respect for human rights and moves to introduce political reform conditions.
The leaders also said the United States and the EU will put the finishing touches next month on a series of agreements that will end barriers on $40 billion worth of trade.

Under the planned mutual recognition agreements, the two sides will agree to recognize the results of each other's testing, inspection and other procedures on a variety of products -- from telecommunications to medical equipment.

"This will remove barriers on $40 billion of trade between the United States and the European Union, cutting red tape for our businesses and prices for our consumers," Clinton said. "One standard, one test, one time."
The White House said in a fact sheet that the two sides had agreed in principle to wrap up negotiations on the agreements by the end of next month.

The areas involved include telecommunications terminal equipment and information technolgy equipment, pharmaceutical good manufacturing practices, medical devices, electromagnetic compatibility, electrical safety and recreational craft.
